Doctorina MedBench: End-to-End Evaluation of Agent-Based
Medical AI
Anna Kozlova1, Stanislau Salavei1, Pavel Satalkin1, Hanna Plotnitskaya1, Sergey Parfenyuk1
1A.I. Doctor Medical Assist LTD, Cyprus
March 2026
Abstract
We present Doctorina MedBench, a comprehensive evaluation framework for agent-based medical AI based on
the simulation of realistic physician–patient interactions. Unlike traditional medical benchmarks that rely on
solving standardized test questions, the proposed approach models a multi-step clinical dialogue in which either a
physician or an AI system must collect medical history, analyze attached materials (including laboratory reports,
images, and medical documents), formulate differential diagnoses, and provide personalized recommendations.
System performance is evaluated using the D.O.T.S. metric, which consists of four components: Diagnosis,
Observations/Investigations, Treatment, and Step Count, enabling assessment of both clinical correctness and
dialogue efficiency.
The system also incorporates a multi-level testing and quality monitoring architecture designed to detect
model degradation during both development and deployment. The framework supports safety-oriented trap cases,
category-based random sampling of clinical scenarios, and full regression testing. The dataset currently contains
more than 1,000 clinical cases covering over 750 diagnoses. The universality of the evaluation metrics allows
the framework to be used not only to assess medical AI systems, but also to evaluate physicians and support the
development of clinical reasoning skills. Our results suggest that simulation of clinical dialogue may provide a
more realistic assessment of clinical competence compared to traditional examination-style benchmarks.

1 Introduction
The rapid advancement of AI and the mounting deficit of healthcare professionals have led to widespread adoption
of AI as a personal health consultant. Despite early skepticism from the medical community, evidence indicates
that physicians are increasingly utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) in their clinical practice. Specifically, in
2024, 66% of doctors reported using AI, marking a 78% increase compared to 2023 [1]. This trajectory is reflected
in the burgeoning number of publications evaluating the performance of AI in medical tasks.
In recent years, numerous studies have investigated AI both as a tool for solving specific medical tasks and for its
ability to substitute for specialist consultations. For example, this includes its application in patient information and
education [2], the capacity to handle specific tasks such as personalized medication selection [3], the development
of decision-support models [4], or fulfilling the role of a physician for the patient [5, 6].
As a result, the question of assessing the quality of such diagnostics and the stability of models is becoming
increasingly relevant. Various performance evaluation systems have been tested; although LLM models have long
been able to solve standard medical tests [7], this does not allow for confident extrapolation of such data to real
clinical cases [8]. Therefore, early methods for comparing AI in medicine relied on benchmarking against expert
opinions, which created certain difficulties. These challenges included the limited productivity of humans who,
unlike LLMs, cannot process hundreds of cases in a short period of time, as well as the presence of the human
factor, which can lead to incorrect interpretation of AI responses.
Consequently, it was concluded that the consensus of multiple specialists is necessary; however, this approach
significantly limits throughput. These constraints prompted the development of fundamentally new AI quality
assessment systems designed to address the challenge of accurately evaluating AI performance across various
medical scenarios. Furthermore, such systems could even facilitate the training of students in clinical reasoning by
simulating realistic clinical cases and patient interactions [9, 10, 11].
However, despite the significant human and economic resources invested in the development of such systems,
they do not fully address all the challenges encountered in creating an evaluation model for an AI physician. In
particular, these approaches only allow for an assessment of the overall performance of an AI physician at a specific
point in time. Furthermore, they remain highly resource-intensive, especially during the development of new
models and the need for continuous testing of even minor modifications.
Given that Doctorina aims to create a fully functional, freely accessible AI physician, there is a need to address
three interrelated tasks within a single system. First, determining the overall quality level of the AI physician during
its development and subsequent improvement. Second, verifying the stability and performance of the AI physician
in real-time. Third, the timely identification and localization of emerging issues, including errors in file processing,
user message translation, and the general logic of the system.
2

2 System Overview
2.1 General Principles of the AI Doctor
The developed AI physician, Doctorina, is a proactive system designed to perform diagnostic assessment and
generate valid recommendations. The system fully replicates the behavior of a real physician during patient
interactions and is neither a symptom checker nor an adapted system to answer specific medical questions.
The mechanism is capable of not only receiving text messages from patients but also processing various types
of attachments—ranging from photographs of body parts to lab results and medical reports—consolidating all
information into a single block for subsequent analysis. Accordingly, Doctorina asks questions guided by clinical
reasoning based on available information, gradually narrowing down the range of potential diseases with each new
patient response.
Doctorina’s objective is to collect all clinically relevant patient data, not only to establish a diagnosis but also
to provide evidence-based recommendations. This ensures more than just the formulation of a probable diagnosis;
it facilitates a multi-stage process of identifying the primary diagnosis and comorbidities through the sequential
exclusion of options from the differential diagnosis. Additionally, the system accounts for factors that influence
the final recommendations, such as family history. Based on this, the system generates final recommendations that
consider all individual characteristics.
The final recommendations include an explanation of the patient’s condition, as well as a personalized diagnostic
plan to confirm or clarify the diagnosis and subsequent treatment. Furthermore, it provides for condition monitoring
with protocols for what to do in case of deterioration, alongside personalized lifestyle advice covering nutrition,
physical activity, habits and sleep hygiene.
2.2 Simulation of the AI-Patient
During the development of a multi-component application such as a generative AI physician, it was found that
traditional evaluation methodologies do not provide a comprehensive and accurate analysis of its effectiveness.
In contrast to standardized examinations, real-world patients rarely provide all pertinent information to medical
professionals spontaneously. Instead, clinicians must actively elicit details, clarify misconceptions, and guide the
patient through the history-taking process before formulating a diagnostic hypothesis or recommendations. To
address this gap, we developed simulation scenarios that more accurately replicate the dynamics of real-world
clinical interactions.
Recent benchmark studies have similarly emphasized that realistic assessment of medical LLMs should extend
beyond static question answering to interactive task environments and rare off-guideline clinical scenarios, where
performance depends on sequential questioning, contextual interpretation, and appropriate use of available evidence
[9], [12].
To evaluate the diagnostic and therapeutic efficacy of the system under realistic conditions, we model physician-
patient interactions using a structured testing mechanism. The simulation operates as a step-by-step cycle with
a defined iteration limit: it begins by adding introductory ”patient” information and optional attachments to the
conversation state, after which the AI physician’s responses are repeatedly fed back into the cycle until the dialogue
is explicitly marked as complete or the predefined step limit is exhausted. This mechanism allows for control over
dialogue length and ensures that completion is determined either by the model itself, when it explicitly reports
primary diagnosis, or as a result of a specified timeout.
The patient behavior is intentionally designed to approximate real clinical consultations, in which clinically
relevant information is often revealed only in response to targeted questioning. This makes the benchmark sensitive
not only to final diagnostic accuracy, but also to the completeness and safety of the physician model’s history-taking
strategy.
The patient’s behavior is intentionally restricted to mimic real clinical consultations. In particular, the simulated
patient does not disclose all clinically relevant details spontaneously; instead, the AI physician must obtain them
through targeted history-taking. This allows the benchmark to measure not only the correctness of the final diagnosis
and recommendations, but also the completeness and safety of the information-gathering process.
The virtual patient is realized as a separate LLM agent governed by a dedicated system prompt. Each benchmark
case is stored as a structured record. During simulation, the patient agent is conditioned on this case record and the
current dialogue history.
The agent is explicitly constrained to behave like a real patient. It answers only the question asked, keeps
responses concise, does not reveal clinically relevant details unless they are specifically elicited, and does not
introduce facts that are absent from the case record. It may paraphrase case facts in natural language, but it is
not allowed to expand them with unsupported symptoms, exposures, diagnoses, or test results. If the physician

asks about information not represented in the case, the patient produces an uncertain or negative reply instead of
hallucinating.
This architecture preserves the linguistic flexibility of an LLM-driven dialogue while maintaining case-level
factual control. Consequently, performance depends on the physician model’s history-taking strategy rather than
on accidental over-disclosure by the simulated patient.
Figure 1: AI Doctor evaluation workflow
The orchestration of each turn is performed by a dialogue module (DoctorModel), which routes messages
between the system’s functional agents. The system logs every step, preserving attachments, tracking completion
flags, and recording model inputs and outputs for subsequent analysis.
Upon completion of a simulated dialogue, the testing mechanism performs a multidimensional evaluation. Four
asynchronous tasks evaluate the dialogue’s completeness, the quality of recommended treatment and history-taking,
and the correctness of prescribed tests and examinations in parallel. The results are structured into an evaluation
record in the DOTS format (Diagnosis, Observations / Investigations, Treatment, Step count), which can be used
to determine ”pass/fail” status for ”trap” cases and for analyzing regression statistics. Test cases and evaluation
logic are housed in a separate module, ensuring that experimental checks cannot influence real patient interactions.
This separation also facilitates safe parallelization and rapid re-runs within continuous integration or real-time
monitoring frameworks.
Future improvements may include explicit modeling of, for example, emergency and routine consultations.
Additionally, stricter step limits for high-complexity scenarios and expanded use of attachments with structured
data are planned to stress-test the system’s ability to extract and correctly utilize information.
Furthermore, the system is flexible, allowing for the simulation of not only the physician-patient dialogue but
also the definition of the patient’s behavioral style. Thus, the simulated patient can not only provide answers to
questions but also provide them with excessive information, insist on specific diagnoses or deny their possibility,
and ask clarifying questions. This is frequently encountered in real-world medical practice when a patient attempts
to convince a doctor of something. As a result, AI patient can mimic behavior not only within a predefined ”medical
case” but also correspond to various behavioral archetypes of real people. After receiving final recommendations,
a scenario is possible where the patient initiates communication to clarify information or report ”forgotten” facts,
necessitating adjustments to previously issued prescriptions.

3 Evaluation Framework
3.1 Core Metrics (D.O.T.S.)
•Diagnosis (D)— accuracy and completeness of the diagnostic solution.
•Observations / Investigations (O)— validity of recommendations for conducting surveys.
•Treatment (T)— safety, adequacy and therapeutic logic.
•Step Count (S)— the number of steps in the dialogue required to make a diagnosis and prescribe treatment.
•Pass thresholds defined for each level (e.g. no critical errors, stage deviations≤20%).
Figure 2: D.O.T.S.
The primary metric for evaluating the performance of the AI physician model is the assessment of outcomes
from a simulated dialogue between a virtual AI patient and an AI physician. The AI patient is provided with baseline
data (an introductory prompt) that initiates the interaction, along with a repository of responses to potential inquiries
within the simulated scenario covering secondary symptoms, medical history (anamnesis), family history, diagnostic
test results, allergies, and current medications. The process culminates in the establishment of a diagnosis by the
AI physician and the provision of primary clinical recommendations.
The AI patient is trained to respond exclusively to the specific questions posed, without volunteering unsolicited
information, which closely mirrors real-world clinical practice. This includes providing data from laboratory and
other diagnostic methods, both at the onset of the interaction and during its course upon the physician’s request.
Additionally, the AI patient can pose clarifying questions to the physician, such as requesting the explanation of
complex medical terminology.
Following the formulation of the diagnosis and recommendations, key performance indicators (KPIs) are
evaluated—specifically: Diagnosis (D), Observations/Investigations (O), Treatment (T), and Step Count (S)—and
compared against the gold standard benchmarks for the given clinical situation.
The Diagnosis (D) indicator comprises two independent metrics: the primary diagnosis itself (the chief
complaint or reason for the virtual patient’s visit) in its textual form, and the corresponding ICD-10 code. The use
of ICD-10 provides a standardized international framework for representing diagnoses and facilitates comparison
across cases. Accurate mapping between standardized medical codes and clinical concepts constitutes an important
and separate dimension of medical LLM evaluation [13]. The application of two or more codes for a single clinical
scenario is permissible. The inclusion of the second metric (ICD-10) accounts for the fact that professional medical
literature often employs diverse terminology to describe the same pathology; for instance, ”pelvic prolapse,” ”pelvic
organ prolapse,” and ”cystocele” may describe the identical clinical situation and correspond to the same ICD-10
code.
The system is verified against both the textual description and the ICD-10 code; a result is deemed unsatisfactory
only if both indicators fail to match simultaneously. Partial discrepancies may be attributed to either synonymy
in diagnostic terminology or the availability of multiple valid ICD-10 codes for primary medical encounters

(e.g., cases involving non-specific symptoms where diagnostic etiology is being clarified alongside the initiation
of treatment). Furthermore, the differential diagnosis list for each clinical scenario is evaluated case-by-case,
specifically measuring the diagnostic accuracy of the Top-3 and Top-5.
Observations / Investigations (O) — This module evaluates the adherence of the model’s diagnostic recom-
mendations to established clinical protocols. Beyond baseline scenarios, complex medical cases may include
data that require adjustments to the diagnostic plan, such as partially completed tests or incidental abnormal
findings unrelated to the primary complaint but requiring further investigation. An example of the latter would
be an abnormal cervical cytology result in a patient with a gastrointestinal disorder. This indicator provides an
integral assessment of diagnostic precision and is composed of three logically distinct components: mandatory
tests (should berecommended), optional or permissible tests (can berecommended), and a penalty system for
redundant or irrelevant orders (unexpected penalty). This structure reflects clinical reality, where investigations
are categorized as essential for diagnosis and patient safety, elective yet justified, or, conversely, unjustified and
excessive.
The first group (mandatory investigations) forms the core of the evaluation. Each element is assigned a weight
reflecting its diagnostic significance. The model receives points only for investigations explicitly mentioned in
its recommendations. Omitting a mandatory test results in the automatic loss of its corresponding weight from
the maximum possible score, thereby objectively documenting any incompleteness in the diagnostic search. The
second group (optional investigations) includes tests that may be appropriate in certain clinical contexts but are not
strictly required. These elements are assigned a weight of zero. Consequently, their presence does not improve
the final score, nor does it diminish it, allowing the model to exhibit clinical variability without risk of penalty.
The third component (unexpected penalty system) is triggered when the model recommends investigations that are
neither mandatory nor optional. Each such entry reduces the final score by a fixed amount, reflecting the real-world
clinical issue of over-testing, which leads to increased healthcare costs, patient burden, and potential procedural
risks. The final output is a percentage score (0–100%) representing the accuracy of the diagnostic recommendations
for a specific case. The Treatment (T) block is analyzed using similar principles, with the addition of a Critical
Condition override. These are predefined criteria which, if triggered, result in the case automatically receiving a
score of zero and a special flag. These conditions identify ”gross medical errors” and are used to monitor for severe
violations, the occurrence of which is modeled artificially. For instance, recommending Amoxicillin to a patient
with a documented penicillin allergy would trigger this override. The purpose of this indicator is to ensure rigorous
control over high-stakes clinical errors, moving beyond simple monitoring of over- or under-prescription.
Step Count (S) represents the number of inquiries initiated by the AI physician before reaching a final diagnosis
and providing recommendations. This metric does not assess the completeness of the clinical interview (captured
by the indicators described above), but rather serves as a behavioral audit of the model.
Large variations in the number of steps may indicate redundant questioning, excessive detail, or improper
grouping of clinical inquiries. A deviation exceeding 25% from the gold standard benchmark, either within a
single case or across identical scenarios is considered a red flag suggesting potential inconsistencies in the model’s
diagnostic reasoning process.

3.2 Evaluator Implementation
Following the completion of each simulated dialogue, the benchmark utilizes an asynchronous evaluation pipeline
comprising four parallel assessment modules: (1) dialogue-level clinical evaluation, (2) history-taking assessment,
(3) treatment-condition verification, and (4) diagnostic-workup checking. These components collectively quantify
performance across multiple dimensions, including Diagnosis, Differential, and ICD-10 Accuracy, as well as
Treatment Proficiency, Question Coverage, and safety-critical pass conditions. The final aggregation of metrics is
executed through a deterministic, case-based framework.
The evaluation engine employs a structured ”LLM-as-a-Judge” architecture. To ensure objectivity, the system
avoids free-form assessment in favor of a schema-validated extraction process. Clinical entities—including primary
and differential diagnoses, recommended investigations, and therapeutic interventions—are identified through
constrained LLM calls using Pydantic-based response formats. Furthermore, ICD-10 codes are normalized from
structured medical data and evaluated using algorithmic code-level matching rules. These extracted outputs are
subsequently processed by deterministic scoring functions that implement weighted diagnostic metrics, mandatory
inquiry coverage, and safety-critical overrides.
6

To mitigate evaluator hallucinations and ensure auditability, the pipeline mandates explicit evidence extraction,
requiring the inclusion of direct dialogue quotations or a ”no evidence” label where information is absent. The
extraction scope is strictly confined to final recommendations to avoid confounding with intermediate reasoning.
By converting natural language inputs into schema-constrained structured data prior to scoring, this hybrid design
balances the linguistic flexibility of LLMs with the reproducibility and rigor required for standardized medical
benchmarking.

4 Multi-Level Testing Protocol and Continuous Monitoring
Continuous Quality Assurance is critical for maintaining the safety and diagnostic reliability of a generative AI
doctor system. To this end, we have implemented a real-time monitoring layer that operates continuously and in
parallel with the production environment. This layer is designed to rapidly identify performance degradations,
often within minutes, while remaining completely isolated from patient interactions.
This layer is intended for the early detection of performance degradation, which can arise in the Doctorina archi-
tecture for several reasons. First, updates to base models or agent routing can alter dialogue behavior, affecting the
thoroughness of history taking and the correctness of clinical reasoning. Second, changes in input data—including
new laboratory report formats, image quality, or user language variability—can reduce the accuracy of extracting
clinically significant information from attachments. Third, degradation may manifest as logic regression in differ-
ential diagnosis or in the formulation of recommendations, as reflected in DOTS metrics (Diagnosis, Observations,
Treatment, Steps). Finally, infrastructure factors (service latency, module routing errors, computational resource
overloads) can disrupt the dialogue cycle sequence and impact the successful completion of clinical scenarios.
These cases are executed at a fixed but adaptive frequency—typically daily—with dynamic rescheduling for
high-priority ”trap cases” or recently failed tests. This strategy ensures system sensitivity to sudden degradations
while minimizing computational costs. Probes are performed across all active model versions, regions, and
languages, providing immediate and comparable performance snapshots.
Each run generates a structured set of metrics, including diagnostic accuracy, the appropriateness of recom-
mended examinations, the adequacy and safety of treatment, and the efficiency of dialogue steps. Additional metrics
track hallucinations, source-grounding errors, attachment parsing quality, routing stability, and translation robust-
ness. These results are automatically aggregated and stratified by clinical category, language, and demographic
context, enabling the early detection of performance drift within specific categories [14].
A key element of the system is the hierarchical escalation mechanism (Fig. 3). If a trap case fails, particularly
in high-risk safety scenarios, the monitoring layer initiates a full Level 3 regression run using the entire case
bank. If these comprehensive tests confirm reproducible degradation, the system automatically notifies clinical
and engineering teams and blocks the promotion of the affected model version until fixes and re-validation are
complete. This cascading architecture ensures that transient fluctuations do not trigger unnecessary shutdowns,
while confirmed failures receive immediate attention.
Figure 3: Real-time Monitoring System Architecture. Short clinical ”trap” test scenarios are executed in parallel
with the production system and evaluated using DOTS metrics. Upon detection of anomalies, a comprehensive
regression run is triggered. If performance degradation is confirmed, the system automatically dispatches notifica-
tions, blocks model promotion, and initiates remediation processes before returning the model to the monitoring
cycle.
Anomaly detection operates on both short-term (sliding one-hour window) and longer twenty-four-hour inter-
vals, comparing metrics against a seven-day median baseline. This approach enables the identification of statistically
significant regressions rather than random outliers. Repeated probe executions are used to assess variance and
confirm instability before escalation, thereby enhancing the reliability of the monitoring circuit.
All monitoring activities are conducted in an isolated evaluation environment, strictly separated from production
data streams to guarantee confidentiality and eliminate any impact on the user experience. System outputs are
visualized in a live dashboard displaying pass rates, severity-weighted safety indices, step efficiency trends, and
category-based heatmaps. Researchers can examine case transcripts, evaluator justifications, and model traces to
accelerate root cause analysis. Weekly reports summarize these results, highlighting regressions, Mean Time to
Detection (MTTD), and remaining coverage gaps.
This real-time quality monitoring layer serves as both an early warning system and a gatekeeping mechanism.
By continuously executing a subset of Level 1 trap cases, transmitting near-real-time signals to Level 2 trend
monitoring, and automatically triggering Level 3 full regression tests upon confirmed anomalies, the system
provides a closed-loop feedback mechanism that maintains diagnostic safety as the model evolves. A detailed
overview of the three-tier evaluation system is provided in the next section.
Originally developed to evaluate the performance of the AI doctor, the system was expanded to meet the need
8

for assessing refinements, tracking improvements, and monitoring overall development. To this end, we proposed
a comprehensive testing approach. This approach includes real-time performance evaluation with rapid failure
response capabilities, as well as a multi-layered assessment of overall system effectiveness.
Furthermore, the evaluation system can be adapted for the training and assessment of medical students and
physicians, specifically to support the development of clinical reasoning and history-taking skills.
4.1 Real-Time Quality Monitoring
As the name implies, these real-time tests are conducted during active system operation to identify potential errors
or anomalous behavior. Their methodology is based on pre-defined scenarios designed to elicit predictable system
responses. This enables instantaneous assessment of model behavior and the immediate detection of failure points
without requiring the completion of a full evaluation cycle.
For instance, testing an image processing module might involve a scenario featuring a child with an infection
lacking ”red flags,” contrasted with a photograph showing a rash characteristic of meningococcal disease. If the
image is evaluated correctly, the system should immediately identify the life-threatening condition without further
inquiry; consequently, any additional questioning by the system is classified as an error.
A second example involves a highly detailed initial patient narrative that provides comprehensive data but omits
two critical pieces of information essential to the clinical context. Evaluation focuses on the system’s next two
sequential queries; if these align precisely with the missing data, the system is deemed to have correctly prioritized
its clinical inquiry. In essence, this testing framework facilitates real-time operational monitoring while enabling
the immediate localization of malfunctioning components.
The second module of the system is designed to evaluate the model’s performance within the framework of
clinical decision-making logic, requiring a comprehensive assessment of all variables. Given the two primary
dilemmas inherent in the process, the evaluation must be efficient, accurate, and resource-conservative. Based on
these criteria, a three-tiered evaluation system is proposed.
4.2 Level 1 – Trap-Based Testing
The first level comprises a limited set of benchmarks designed to elicit errors in both human clinicians and AI models.
These scenarios include complex clinical cases as well as ”intentional misleading” situations, where a patient
might directly deny a potential condition or provide conflicting information rooted in genuine misconceptions. For
example, a patient may deny the possibility of pregnancy due to a history of infertility or prior surgical interventions,
while simultaneously describing classic symptoms of the condition. Such cases should not distract the clinician
from the diagnosis or lead to its premature dismissal without rigorous clinical reasoning. Essentially, level-one
benchmarks are a curated selection of ”must-pass” tests required for system deployment. These tests span all
modules of the AI physician, providing a comprehensive assessment of its operational accuracy.
4.3 Level 2 – Category-Based Random Sampling
Given that modern evaluation datasets comprise thousands of cases, their concurrent execution not only inflates
development costs but also significantly bottlenecks the development workflow, as engineers must wait for the
full evaluation cycle to conclude. Our proposed alternative involves selecting a fixed number of cases from each
category at random, with the mandatory inclusion of cases that scored below 70% in prior testing at this level. This
approach facilitates rapid feedback for the technical team while minimizing expenditures. The implementation of
a specialized dashboard enables the tracking of metric dynamics (D.O.T.S.) across recurring cases, simplifying
visual interpretation and optimizing developer time. Upon achieving satisfactory results at Level 2, the evaluation
progresses to the complete dataset.
4.4 Level 3 – Full Regression Testing
Meta-evaluation of the Assessment Framework (Error Testing): Since the reliability of results depends heavily on
the integrity of the scoring system, we incorporate tests containing intentional errors. For example, a scenario
might list certain medications as ”necessary” when half of them are actually contraindicated in that specific clinical
context. Consequently, a correctly performed evaluation of such a case should result in D.O.T.S. metrics decreasing
by a predetermined value. Any deviation from these expected lower scores—including the attainment of high
scores—indicates a malfunction within the evaluation system itself.

5 Case Design and Dataset Management
5.1 Source and Maintenance of Cases
The current dataset was developed by a group of physicians utilizing their expert knowledge and consultation logs
from individuals who engaged with the Doctorina platform during its prototype testing phase, with their informed
consent.
Each case underwent validation by at least two physicians, who assessed the clinical realism of the scenarios,
the accuracy of the primary and differential diagnoses, and the validity of the diagnostic and treatment recommen-
dations. Particular emphasis was placed on assigning ”weights” to recommendations within each case. In this
context, weighting refers to the contribution of a specific recommendation to the overall score on a scale of 0 to
100. For instance, the prescription of a specific medication (e.g., levofloxacin) might contribute up to 80% of the
score in one clinical scenario, whereas it may account for only 20% in another.
The dataset comprises over 1,000 clinical cases that cover more than 750 unique diagnoses. The gender
distribution among cases with specified sex is nearly balanced, with 51.28% females and 48.72% males. Based
on broad clinical categories, the distribution is as follows: internal medicine (50.53%), obstetrics and gynecology
(16.70%), pediatrics (16.25%), and surgery (16.52%). Consequently, more than half of the database consists of
internal medicine cases, alongside significant proportions of gynecological and pediatric cases.

The construction of the dataset and the balancing of categories were modeled after the official structure of the

5.2 Treatment Evaluation Logic. Categorization of tests.
Each test has two levels of categorization.
5.2.1 Level 1 – ”Category” Conditions
Each base test is assigned a single category, which is inherited by all subsequent versions. This categorization
determines the ’weight’ of each medical discipline during the testing process. Changes identified during tests are
monitored to evaluate prompt versions, ensuring that there is no degradation in performance quality across specific
disciplines. The total test count is determined exclusively by the category.
The number of categories is fixed:Internal medicine, Pediatrics, Surgery, Oncology, Obstetrics and Gyne-
cology, Psychiatry, Emergency Medicine, Error Tests.
5.2.2 Level 2 – ”Scope” Conditions
A single clinical case can encompass multiple variations, including those assigned to different categories. These
variations may differ between the baseline test and subsequent modifications, as new versions may be added and
original ones removed. The only exception is the ’Technical’ category; only one such scope can exist within a
single test.
Tests are initiated at the Scope level, and execution by ’Category’ is also supported. However, tests in the
’Technical’ category are never executed under any circumstances.

Question difficulty level tags:
A) Basic Level
Key focus:solitary, uncomplicated pathology without concomitant diseases.
Characteristics:
•One diagnosis (eg, uncomplicated cystitis, viral pharyngitis)
•Typical symptoms with a clear clinical picture
•Minimum amount of laboratory data
•A simple and straightforward logical chain: “complaint→diagnosis→treatment”
Skills:recognition of typical clinical patterns, basic differential diagnosis.
B) Intermediate Level
Key focus:ambiguous clinical picture or the presence of mild concomitant pathology.
Characteristics:
•One primary disease and one secondary condition (e.g., diabetes mellitus + urinary tract infection)
•Overlapping symptoms requiring interpretation of laboratory data
•Possible non-obvious causes (for example, anemia in a woman with menorrhagia)
Skills:integration of data from multiple sources, hypothesis formation, decision making under conditions of
incomplete information.
C) Advanced Level
Key focus:multiple concomitant diseases or complicated course of the disease.Characteristics:
•Two or three chronic medical conditions that affect the current condition (e.g., chronic heart failure,
chronic kidney disease, and pneumonia)
•Unobvious drug interactions and contraindications
•The need to consider pathophysiological relationships and limitations of therapy
•Possible laboratory abnormalities requiring interpretation
Skills:clinical thinking, problem prioritization, balancing therapeutic decisions.
D) Expert / Complex Reasoning Level
Key focus:diagnostic uncertainty, rare or atypical clinical manifestations.
Characteristics:
•Involvement of multiple body systems (e.g., systemic autoimmune diseases)
•Conflicting data or atypical course of the disease
•The need to exclude several differential diagnoses
•Possible presence of rare conditions, syndromes, or secondary complications (e.g., LADA, paraneo-
plastic syndrome)
Skills:analytical thinking, constructing a diagnostic tree, forming an examination plan, probabilistic thinking.
This level is intended to capture forms of reasoning that are especially relevant in benchmark settings focused
on expert-level medical understanding, diagnostic uncertainty, and rare off-guideline cases [12, 15] .

A key principle in the construction of the dataset was the distribution of cases across both broad clinical
categories (such as internal medicine, surgery, and obstetrics and gynecology) and specific medical disciplines.
Particular emphasis was placed on maintaining a balanced representation of patient demographics (sex and age)
and varying levels of clinical scenario complexity. We aim to maintain a distribution structure comparable to the
United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE); the current dataset reflects the following proportions
across clinical disciplines. Furthermore, emergency medicine was designated as a distinct category to facilitate the
independent testing of scenarios requiring rapid clinical decision-making by the model.
•Medicine — 50–60% of all questions
•Surgery — 25–30%
•Pediatrics — 20–25%
•Obstetrics & Gynecology — 10–20%
•Psychiatry — 10–15%

structure of the USMLE Step 2 CK examination. Within the exam, questions are distributed as follows:

7 Discussion
As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to evolve, the use of standardized test items as the primary criterion for
their medical performance has become increasingly problematic. This is due to the fact that achieving maximum
scores on such tests does not correlate with the successful execution of simulation tasks approximating real-
world clinical practice - a phenomenon repeatedly demonstrated across a series of publications [16, 8, 17, 18].
Historically, the introduction of test items was intended to minimize subjectivity in knowledge assessment and
ensure the objectivity of the examination process. However, LLMs are inherently unaffected by human factors
during evaluation; consequently, this specific objective is losing its relevance. This raises a critical question: when
will standardized tests for medical students be replaced by formats more closely aligned with clinical practice,
including simulation-based methods for assessing knowledge levels?
To validate the robustness of our evaluation framework, we conducted a comparative experiment involving
three general practitioners (GPs) across 100 clinical cases. These scenarios represented baseline medical instances,
characterized by typical disease presentations and an absence of comorbidities. The results demonstrated that
human performance metrics were closely aligned with those of AI Doctor, with clinicians achieving a Diagnosis
Accuracy of 83% compared to 87% for the specialized model. This parity confirms the framework’s efficacy in
accurately evaluating both human practitioners and domain-specific Large Language Models (LLMs).
In contrast, the GPT-5 baseline, utilizing a restricted single-sentence prompt, demonstrated a diagnostic accuracy
of 81.0% on the identical dataset. This configuration served as a deliberate control to isolate the foundation model’s
inherent reasoning from the performance gains introduced by Doctorina’s specialized architecture, specifically its
multi-agent design, structured anamnesis protocols, and safety-centric orchestration. These findings underscore
that Doctorina’s integrated framework achieves superior diagnostic alignment with clinical expertise compared to
standard, general-purpose LLM architectures.
Given that modern LLM systems are frequently benchmarked against practicing physicians in comparative
analyses of test-solving and clinical case management, including complex diagnostic scenarios, this research
direction appears methodologically significant. To this end, the system we developed was integrated to facilitate user
interaction through instant messaging. This approach replicates the format of written doctor-patient communication,
where the content of the response is directly contingent upon the precision of the inquiry. Such a methodology
reduces the probability of inadvertently obtaining critical information and, by extension, arriving at a coincidental
diagnosis. For instance, a patient may initially report blood pressure readings from only one arm; however, through
meticulous questioning and a request for a bilateral measurement, they provide the additional data necessary for an
accurate assessment.

8 Conclusion
The results of this study call into question the widespread use of standardized test benchmarks as the primary
tool for evaluating medical artificial intelligence. Although modern large language models (LLMs) are capable
of meeting or even exceeding human performance on medical board examination tasks, such as the USMLE,
these results do not fully reflect their competence in real-world clinical settings. Our work confirms that when
a physician-modeled diagnostic task is integrated into an interactive clinical simulation mimicking a real doctor-
patient dialogue and requiring structured history taking, reasoning under conditions of incomplete information,
and maintaining a dynamic conversation the performance of base LLMs drops sharply compared to practicing
physicians. This performance gap becomes even more pronounced in simulations involving multiple conditions or
patients with comorbidities.
At the same time, the findings indicate that systemic approaches integrating LLM capabilities into structured
clinical reasoning frameworks can significantly enhance diagnostic efficiency. The developed system, ”Doctorina,”
demonstrates nearly identical accuracy to medical specialists in basic medical scenarios and superior accuracy in
cases involving comorbidity, significantly outperforming base LLM models.
In this paper, we have presented a framework for clinical simulation based on expert-developed scenarios,
designed to evaluate medical reasoning in conditions close to real clinical practice. Unlike traditional benchmarks
based on static test questions, the proposed approach evaluates the ability to obtain relevant clinical information
through structured interviewing, reason under data incompleteness, and iteratively refine diagnostic hypotheses
during the doctor-patient interaction. Such systems are essential both as more realistic benchmarks for evaluating
medical AI and as educational environments for developing history-taking and clinical reasoning skills.
Several limitations of the study should be noted. A rigorous comparison of LLM systems with medical
specialists requires the use of independently generated clinical datasets developed by external expert groups to
minimize potential researcher bias. Furthermore, practical constraints substantially limit the number of clinical
cases that can be analyzed by human physicians, whereas LLMs are capable of processing significantly larger
datasets. Finally, unlike general-purpose LLMs, physicians possess highly specialized expertise; this necessitates
a careful alignment of clinical cases with the specific areas of specialization of the participating experts.

This partial document describes the "AI Doctor" system, named Doctorina, focusing on its general principles and the simulation methodology used for its evaluation.

*   **Information Processing:** Doctorina can process text messages and various attachments (photos, lab results, medical reports) to consolidate information for analysis.
*   **Diagnostic Process:** The system uses clinical reasoning to ask targeted questions, narrowing down potential diseases. It aims to collect all clinically relevant data to establish a primary diagnosis, identify comorbidities, and consider factors like family history for personalized, evidence-based recommendations.
*   **Recommendation Content:** Final recommendations include an explanation of the condition, a personalized diagnostic and treatment plan, condition monitoring protocols (including what to do in case of deterioration), and personalized lifestyle advice (nutrition, exercise, habits, sleep).
*   **Simulation Methodology:** Traditional evaluation methods are insufficient for generative AI physicians. A simulation of AI-patient interactions is used to replicate real-world clinical dynamics where patients don't spontaneously provide all information.
*   **Simulation Design:** The simulation involves a step-by-step cycle where the AI physician's responses are fed back. It begins with initial patient information and attachments, and the dialogue continues until completion or a step limit is reached.
*   **Patient Simulation:** The virtual patient is an LLM agent designed to mimic real patient behavior, only revealing clinically relevant information when specifically asked, thus testing the AI physician's history-taking strategy for completeness and safety.
*   **Evaluation Focus:** The benchmark is sensitive to both final diagnostic accuracy and the quality of the information-gathering process.

This partial document describes a multi-level testing protocol and continuous monitoring system designed to ensure the quality, safety, and diagnostic reliability of a generative AI doctor system. The system includes a real-time monitoring layer that operates in parallel with the production environment to quickly detect performance degradations. These degradations can stem from various factors, including updates to AI models, changes in input data formats, logic regressions in clinical reasoning, and infrastructure issues.

The testing protocol is structured in three levels:

*   **Level 1 – Trap-Based Testing:** This level uses a limited set of challenging "trap cases" and "intentional misleading" scenarios designed to identify critical errors in both human clinicians and AI models. These are considered "must-pass" tests for system deployment.
*   **Level 2 – Category-Based Random Sampling:** This level involves randomly selecting a fixed number of cases from each clinical category for rapid feedback, including cases that previously scored poorly. This approach balances efficiency with comprehensive assessment.
*   **Level 3 – Full Regression Testing:** This level involves running the entire case bank to confirm reproducible degradations identified in lower levels.

The system features a hierarchical escalation mechanism where failures in trap cases can trigger more comprehensive testing. If degradation is confirmed, the system automatically notifies relevant teams and blocks the promotion of affected model versions. Anomaly detection uses short-term and long-term intervals to identify statistically significant regressions. All monitoring occurs in an isolated environment, with results visualized on a live dashboard and summarized in weekly reports. The document also suggests the potential adaptation of this evaluation system for training medical professionals.

This partial document focuses on the evaluation results, visualization, and trend monitoring of a medical AI system. It details aggregated scoring and trend analysis, explaining how mean metric values are used to assess performance across different medical specialties and identify potential model bias. The document outlines various accuracy metrics, including Diagnosis Accuracy, Differential Accuracy, Treatment Accuracy, and Diagnostic Accuracy, both on average and within specific categories. It also presents interaction statistics like total steps and cases outside a soft step limit.

The document then describes a visualization system that uses histograms to represent system quality profiles, interpreting metrics in context with related indicators. It explains how test cases are structured with unique IDs, categories, tags, and detailed diagnostic information. A significant portion is dedicated to a comparative performance analysis between a GPT-5 baseline and a specialized AI Doctor system, detailing the methodology for establishing the baseline and the specific metrics used for comparison. The document defines and explains the calculation of several key metrics, including Question Accuracy, Diagnosis Accuracy, ICD-10 Accuracy, Differential Accuracy, Treatment Accuracy, Diagnostic Accuracy, Critical Conditions Passed, Conversation Completion Rate, Total Steps, Average Steps, and Cases outside ±25% of steps soft limit. Finally, it presents a comparative analysis of diagnostic metrics, highlighting that the AI Doctor system generally outperformed the GPT-5 baseline in areas like Diagnosis Accuracy, Differential Accuracy, and Question Accuracy, while GPT-5 had a higher weighted Diagnostic Accuracy score.

structure.title: Statistical Evaluation of Model Version Updates
structure.summary:
The partial document discusses a comparative analysis between a specialized AI Doctor model and a general-purpose GPT-5 model in medical dialogue and diagnosis. Key points covered include:

*   **Dialogue Metrics:** AI Doctor facilitates significantly more extensive clinical interactions, with a higher number of total and average doctor-patient turns compared to GPT-5. AI Doctor also shows greater consistency in dialogue length.
*   **Statistical Evaluation of Model Updates:** A statistical evaluation using metrics like diagnosis accuracy, treatment accuracy, and differential accuracy was performed.
*   **Treatment Accuracy:** AI Doctor showed improvements in treatment accuracy in a significant portion of cases compared to GPT-5, with an overall positive shift in recommendations.
*   **Diagnosis Accuracy:** McNemar's test indicated a statistically significant improvement in diagnosis accuracy for AI Doctor, correcting more errors than it introduced.
*   **Other Metrics:** Critical condition detection and conversation completion showed no statistically significant differences between the models.
*   **Average Metric Changes:** AI Doctor demonstrated substantial increases in diagnostic and treatment accuracy, differential diagnosis accuracy, and dialogue length, while diagnostic testing accuracy decreased.
*   **Human Performance Comparison:** The AI Doctor model's performance metrics were closely aligned with those of human general practitioners in a comparative experiment, suggesting its robustness and clinical relevance.
*   **Impact of Prompting:** The document highlights how the precision of inquiries significantly influences diagnostic outcomes, even with baseline LLM models.

structure.title: Discussion
structure.summary: The provided document excerpt discusses the limitations of standardized tests for evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) in medical contexts, arguing that simulation-based assessments better reflect real-world clinical practice. It presents a comparative experiment where a specialized LLM ("AI Doctor" or "Doctorina") and human general practitioners (GPs) achieved similar diagnostic accuracy on baseline clinical cases. The excerpt highlights that a general-purpose LLM (GPT-5) with a restricted prompt performed less accurately, underscoring the benefits of Doctorina's specialized architecture. It emphasizes the importance of precise questioning in LLM-based medical assessments, as demonstrated by patient response variations to different inquiries. The document contrasts the performance of LLMs in their system with their performance on standardized tests like the USMLE, where LLMs have previously outperformed physicians. Finally, it presents comparative performance metrics for obstetricians and gynecologists against various LLM models within their system, showing Doctorina outperforming both human specialists and basic LLM versions. The excerpt concludes by positioning the developed system as a valuable tool for training medical professionals and evaluating LLMs, facilitating the analysis of LLM integration into healthcare.

structure.title: Conclusion
structure.summary: This partial document, a conclusion section, argues that standardized test benchmarks are insufficient for evaluating medical AI, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs). While LLMs perform well on static medical exams like the USMLE, their performance significantly declines in interactive clinical simulations that mimic real doctor-patient dialogues, require structured history taking, and involve incomplete information or comorbidities. The document highlights a system called "Doctorina" which, by integrating LLM capabilities into structured clinical reasoning frameworks, achieves comparable or superior diagnostic accuracy to medical specialists. The authors propose this simulation-based framework as a more realistic benchmark for medical AI and an educational tool. Limitations include the need for independent datasets to avoid bias, the practical constraints on human physician analysis compared to LLMs, and the challenge of aligning LLM capabilities with specialized medical expertise.
